ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Cardiology Referral — Zora Neale Hurston

code.originalText: Establishing care for morning headaches, breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling, with very high blood pressure: examination, ECG, laboratory tests, 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, a two-drug combination, food and medicine-cost screening, and stroke warning signs

text.paragraph: Breathlessness on exertion, mild ankle swelling and stage 2 blood pressure in a 67-year-old woman, with left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG and a raised NT-proBNP. Please confirm whether this is hypertensive heart disease with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, exclude its mimics, and advise on treatment. [S]
Urgency: Soon; on the day of her two-week visit, after the echocardiogram that morning. [S]

list.item: Is the breathlessness due to hypertensive heart disease with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction?
Are there features of a mimic or another cause, such as cardiac amyloidosis, valve disease or coronary disease, and does she need further testing?
Is chlorthalidone with amlodipine the right combination for her, and what blood pressure target do you advise?
Which heart failure medicines do you recommend, and in what order, given her costs?
What is her stroke risk, and does she need screening for atrial fibrillation?

text.paragraph: Writer, anthropologist and substitute teacher with a low and irregular income; Original Medicare without drug coverage; no car. Two months of morning headaches and three months of breathlessness on one flight of stairs, with ankle swelling by evening. Clinic blood pressure 178/104 and 174/102 mmHg without signs of a hypertensive emergency; fundi with arteriolar narrowing and nicking, no hemorrhage or papilledema; neurological examination normal. ECG: sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage with repolarization changes, no Q waves. NT-proBNP 480 pg/mL; creatinine 0.88 mg/dL (eGFR 72), potassium 3.9 mmol/L; hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL; TSH 1.9; hemoglobin A1c 5.6%; LDL 132 mg/dL; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 22 mg/g. A 24-hour ambulatory recording was fitted today. Plan: chlorthalidone 12.5 mg and amlodipine 5 mg from tomorrow, low-cost generics. Never smoker; alcohol rarely. She asks that every choice be explained and its cost considered [S]

list.item: She wants to keep teaching, writing and gardening, and to get her breath back. [S]
She cannot afford expensive medicines or extra trips, and food runs short at the end of the month. [S]
She wants her own account of her symptoms to be believed and every choice explained. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Zora Neale Hurston was born on January 7, 1891, in Notasulga, Alabama, the fifth of eight children of John Hurston, a carpenter and Baptist preacher, and Lucy Potts Hurston, a former schoolteacher. [D]
She was born as Zora Lee Hurston, according to the Florida Artists Hall of Fame. [D]

Her family moved to Eatonville, Florida, the nation's first incorporated Black township, when she was a toddler (at about three, in 1894), and her father later became its mayor; for her, Eatonville was always home. [D]
Her mother died in 1904, when Zora was 13. [D]

In 1917, aged 26 and needing to present herself as a teenager to qualify for free public schooling in Baltimore, she gave her age as 16 and her birth year as 1901; from then on she presented herself as at least ten years younger than she was. The headstone placed on her grave in 1973 reads 1901. [D]

She attended Howard University and Barnard College, where she studied anthropology with Franz Boas and received a bachelor of arts degree in 1928; she did folklore field work in the South and became a writer and anthropologist of the Harlem Renaissance. [D]
Over more than 30 years she published four novels, including Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), two books of folklore, an autobiography, and many stories, essays, articles and plays. [D]
She never received the financial rewards her work deserved; the largest royalty she earned from any of her books was $943.75. [D]
In 1950 she worked as a maid in Florida while still publishing in national magazines, and she struggled to find work throughout the 1950s. [D]

She worked as a librarian at Patrick Air Force Base in Florida (from June 1956 by one account, for about a year by another) and then moved to Fort Pierce, where she wrote a column on "Hoodoo and Black Magic" for the Fort Pierce Chronicle from 1957 to 1959; a family friend from Eatonville invited her to live in a small house in Fort Pierce rent-free. [D]
In 1958 she worked as a substitute teacher at Lincoln Park Academy in Fort Pierce. [D]
Rarely a drinker, she was remembered by friends for her humor and storytelling and for the gift of walking into hearts. [D]

list.item: Writer, folklorist and anthropologist trained at Barnard; now works as a substitute teacher at the local high school and writes a weekly newspaper column; working on a new book [S]
Lives alone in a small house in Fort Pierce that a friend from her hometown lets her live in without rent; keeps a garden and a dog; no car, walks or takes the bus; no air conditioning, only fans [S]

Income: daily substitute-teaching pay when called and small payments for her column, plus a small Social Security benefit; book royalties have been small; Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) with no drug plan and no supplemental coverage, because she could not afford the premiums [S]
Diet: home cooking with salt pork, greens, rice, fish and cornbread; canned foods at the end of the month when money runs short; adds salt at the table [S]
Tobacco: never. Alcohol: rarely, a glass at a celebration. No drug use [S]

Strengths and supports: raised in Eatonville, an all-Black town she calls home; a lifelong collector of stories; describes a wide circle of friends, students and neighbors, and a sense of humor she relies on [S]
Says she has often had to insist on being taken seriously, and asks that her account of her own body be believed and that every choice be explained to her as to a colleague [S]

Respectful, shared decision-making: take her history as given, explain each test and medicine with its reasons and alternatives, write the plan down, and check costs with her before prescribing. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025) [S]

Confirm the diagnosis with 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring today, before the first dose; then home readings twice daily with a validated upper-arm monitor and a large cuff lent by the clinic. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension and heart failure monographs (2026) [S]

Start a two-drug combination for stage 2 hypertension: chlorthalidone 12.5 mg and amlodipine 5 mg every morning, from the morning after the ambulatory monitor is removed, as low-cost generics; target below 130/80 mmHg; less salt, using foods she already eats. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension and heart failure monographs (2026) [S]

Baseline tests: ECG, NT-proBNP, metabolic panel and magnesium, hemoglobin, TSH, hemoglobin A1c, lipids, ALT and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; echocardiogram because of raised NT-proBNP, breathlessness and suspected left ventricular hypertrophy. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension and heart failure monographs (2026) [S]

Stroke and emergency warning signs: BE FAST (balance, eyes, face, arm, speech, time to call 911), and call 911 for chest pain, severe headache with confusion or vision loss, or breathlessness at rest. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); Signs and Symptoms of Stroke (2026) [S]

Costs and coverage, with the clinic's community health worker: a SHINE counselor for Extra Help and the Medicare Savings Program; generic medicines in 90-day fills; patient assistance for any brand-only medicine until coverage begins. Guideline: Help with drug costs (Extra Help) (2026); Medicare Savings Programs (2026); SHINE (Serving Health Insurance Needs of Elders), Florida's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (2026) [S]

Food: the Hunger Vital Sign at intake; help applying for SNAP through ACCESS Florida; the food pantry list. Guideline: The Hunger Vital Sign (2026); SNAP Eligibility (2026); Public Assistance (ACCESS Florida: SNAP, Medicaid and Medicare Savings Programs) (2026) [S]
